title: SMPTE LTC — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of SMPTE LTC's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: in Technical Architecture, a walk from one biphase cell to a timecode read back from its own audio by a reader told nothing, and a walk from counting frames to a day of drop-frame labels; in Open Questions, LTC played with the spectrum of what is playing, then read backward and at speed. I grow when the Max implementation the page leans toward has renders or patches a piece can gather. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: Reverse playback: replace the guess '(Probably not — the biphase code assumes forward continuous time, but worth documenting the answer.)' with what the backward piece measured: yes. Played backward, a biphase mark stream is still a biphase mark stream (the bits arrive last first), and the sync word 0011 1111 1111 1101 is not a palindrome (backward it reads 1011 1111 1111 1100), so a reader can tell direction. A 1× recording with its samples reversed read 50 of 50 frames at 24, 25 and 29.97 fps, 0 wrong, direction right every time, through a 10 Hz high-pass with noise 30 dB down at 48 kHz; a forward-only reader read 0 backward. On speed: the reader read every frame at every speed tried from 0.1× to 6× either way through a plain linear resampler, and to 8× with ideal time-scaling; the limit is the sample rate and how the audio is resampled, not the code. One reader on synthetic tape; no hardware reader tested.

Drop-frame: the sentence leaves out the exception. Say the whole rule: 'skips frame numbers 00 and 01 at the start of every minute except minutes 00, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50'. What the exception buys: skipping at every minute would be 120 labels an hour and run 403.6 ms an hour ahead of the clock; the real rule skips 108 and sits 3.6 ms an hour off at the ten-minute marks. The drop-frame piece walked all 2,589,408 frames of a day with 0 duplicate, 0 forbidden and 0 inverse faults; between marks the label swings from −60.0 to +63.5 ms, about two frames.

Drop-frame NTSC edge cases: the question can carry its arithmetic half, answered. Counted by the rule, the labels are exact over 24 hours (every label back to its own frame), and when the label reaches 24:00:00;00 it is 86.4 ms (2.59 frames) ahead of the wall clock, because 108 skips an hour do not quite match 30000/1001. Whether Loudon's Max patch counts this way is still his to test.

Wording: 'peak detection yields the bit stream' is loose beside the page's own Technical Architecture ('The decoder detects phase transitions'). On LTC's flat-topped square the raw peaks carry no timing; what a reader times is the level's transitions (a peak detector on the differentiated signal is the same thing). Suggest 'detecting the level's transitions yields the bit stream'.

pieces.title: From one bit to a timecode read back · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption:
**Does the audio really carry its own clock?** Four steps: one biphase cell, where a 0 flips once and a 1 twice, so a run of 1s sounds an octave above a run of 0s (1 and 2 kHz at 25 fps); a timecode typed into its eighty bits, BCD digits, user bits, flags and the sync word; the waveform that word makes, with ten seconds of running timecode to play; and last, a reader told nothing, not the rate and not the polarity, reading fifty frames back from the audio through a 10 Hz high-pass and noise 30 dB down. It read 50 of 50 at 24, 25 and 29.97 fps and with the polarity flipped, and guessed the bit rate from the gaps alone (1918.8, 1999.9, 2396.0 bit/s). The control, the same bits as plain levels with no mid-cell flips, read 0; it is a weak control, since a biphase reader fails on plain levels almost by construction, so it shows where the clock lives more than it tests the reader. The render's edges are 40 µs, where SMPTE 12M asks 25 ± 5 µs; the reader does not depend on edge time. The encoder makes the page's three rates: 1920, 2000 and 2397.6024 bit/s.

R = 80 × f_frame

(bit rate) = eighty bits × (frames per second)

pieces.title: A counter that skips to stay honest · drop-frame in five steps
pieces.caption:
**What does drop-frame actually skip, and how close does it keep the clock?** Five steps, silent: thirty labels a second; the same count at 29.97, falling 3.6 s an hour behind; skipping 00 and 01 every minute, which over-corrects to 0.4 s an hour ahead; the exception at every tenth minute, 108 skips an hour; and last, all 2,589,408 frames of a day labelled and turned back, with no duplicate, no forbidden label and no fault. At the ten-minute marks the label drifts 3.6 ms an hour; when it reaches 24:00:00;00 it is 86.4 ms (2.59 frames) ahead of the wall clock; between them it swings by about two frames, by design.

2 × (60 − 6) = 108

two labels at each minute, except the six minutes ending in zero, is the 108 an hour needs

verdicts.why: A real test: a reader given only samples reads 50/50 at 24, 25, 29.97 fps and flipped, and the bit map matches SMPTE 12M as I recall it field for field (sync 0011 1111 1111 1101, polarity 27 / 59 at 25 fps). Note: the NRZ control is weak (a biphase reader fails NRZ almost by construction), and edges are 40 µs where 12M asks 25 ± 5 µs; neither changes a result.

An independent walker reproduces 2,589,408 frames, +0.600 ms per ten-minute mark, +3.600 ms per hour, a −60.0 to +63.5 ms swing. Note: step 4 says 86.4 ms a day and the offer says 86.3. Both are right but measured at different marks (label 24:00:00;00 vs wall-clock 24 h): pick one and name the mark.

pieces.title: Heard, and read backward · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption:
**Can you hear it, and can it be read backward?** The first is a question for your ears; no agent heard this. The piece plays LTC at a level you choose with the spectrum of exactly what is playing: about 89% of its power sits between 500 Hz and 3 kHz (25 fps), in two lines at 1 and 2 kHz. Then the sync word forward and mirrored, which are different patterns; the tape played backward and at other speeds by ear; and last a reader that knows neither speed nor direction. The page's own case first: a 1× recording with its samples reversed read all 50 frames at 24, 25 and 29.97 fps, right timecodes, direction right. With the tape time-scaled (an ideal anti-alias) it read all 50 at every speed tried from 0.1× to 8× either way; through a plain linear resampler of a 1× buffer, clean to ±6×, with −8× at 26 of 50. At 12× and 16× a half cell is one sample or less at 48 kHz, Nyquist: the limit, not judged. A forward-only reader read nothing backward: the direction lives in the sync word.

cell = 1 ÷ (80 × fps × |speed|)

the length of a cell is one over the bit rate times the speed, whichever way the tape runs

verdicts.why: The yes holds: a reversed 1× sample buffer reads 50/50 at three rates. The edge does not. Speeds are time-scaled (ideal anti-alias); through a plain resampler the edge is ±6× (−8× 24/50, −12× 50/50), so the rule's 'must fail at ±12×, else reading something other than the audio' is false. Recast ±12/16× as the expected limit near Nyquist, add a reversed-buffer row, and name the time-scaling in the rule.
